# Moving Data Around {#chp:data}

Sooner or later you need to hand data to something that is not R: a web page,
a JavaScript library, or an HTML file that must carry its own attachments.
This chapter covers two encodings that make that easy, JSON and base64.

## Encode and decode base64 {#sec:base64}

`base64_encode()` and `base64_decode()` convert between raw bytes and base64
strings. `base64_uri()` goes one step further and makes a data URI, which embeds
a file directly in HTML. It is the mechanism behind `xfun::embed_file()`:

```{r}
raw_bytes = charToRaw("Hello, xfun!")
(b64 = base64_encode(raw_bytes))
rawToChar(base64_decode(b64))

# data URI for a small file
f = system.file("LICENSE", package = "xfun")
substr(base64_uri(f), 1, 60)
```

## Turn R objects into JSON {#sec:tojson}

`tojson()` converts R objects to JSON (or JavaScript). Named lists become
objects, unnamed lists become arrays, matrices go by row, and data frames go
by column:

```{r}
tojson(list(x = 1:3, y = c(TRUE, FALSE), z = NULL))
tojson(head(iris, 3))   # data frame: columns
tojson(matrix(1:6, 2))  # matrix: rows
```

## Embed JavaScript in the JSON {#sec:js}

Need a callback in your configuration? Wrap a string in `js()` and it is
written as raw JavaScript, with no quotes:

```{r}
tojson(list(n = 42, callback = js("function(x) { return x * 2; }")))
```

## Get strict JSON {#sec:json-mode}

By default the output is JavaScript, which can contain things that JSON does
not allow. For output that is valid for `JSON.parse()`, use `mode = "json"`.
Dates become strings and `Inf` becomes `null`:

```{r}
tojson(list(d = Sys.Date(), x = c(1, Inf, -Inf)), mode = "json")
```

## Shrink repeated values {#sec:dict}

When a vector repeats the same few values many times, `dict` encodes it as an
index plus a list of unique values, which can be much shorter:

```{r}
x = rep(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), 100)
nchar(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE))            # without dict encoding
nchar(tojson(x, dict = 1, pretty = FALSE))  # with dict encoding
```

## Convert a single vector to JSON {#sec:json-vector}

`tojson()` handles whole objects. For one atomic vector, `json_vector()` is the
building block underneath. It returns the elements as strings (quoted by
default, `NA` becomes `null`), or a single array string with `to_array = TRUE`:

```{r}
json_vector(c("a", "b", NA))
json_vector(c("a", "b", NA), to_array = TRUE)
json_vector(c(1, NA, Inf), to_array = TRUE, quote = FALSE)
```

## Ship big integer vectors compactly {#sec:json-pack}

Long integer vectors can be packed as base64 with `tojson(pack = n)`, where `n`
is the minimum length to pack. In `mode = "json"` the output is still valid
JSON, and much shorter than the plain array:

```{r}
x = list(a = 1:200)
nchar(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE))
nchar(tojson(x, pack = 10, mode = "json", pretty = FALSE))
```

The browser needs to turn the base64 string back into a typed array. That is
what `json_unpack` and `json_reviver` are for. Both are plain character strings
of JavaScript, ready to paste into a `<script>`.

## Unpack packed values in the browser {#sec:json-unpack}

`json_unpack` defines a JavaScript function `unpack(o)` that decodes one packed
object on demand. Use it when you parse the JSON yourself and want to unpack
only the fields you need:

```{r}
cat(json_unpack)
```

## Revive packed values while parsing {#sec:json-reviver}

`json_reviver` includes `unpack()` and also defines `reviver`, so
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` expands packed and dictionary-encoded values
automatically as it parses (`tojson(dict = 1, mode = "json")` produces the
latter). Prefer `unpack()` for large payloads, since a reviver runs on every
parsed value:

```{r}
substr(json_reviver, nchar(json_unpack) + 2, nchar(json_reviver))
```

## Read simple YAML without dependencies {#sec:taml-load}

`taml_load()` parses TAML, a tiny subset of YAML (scalars, one-level nesting,
and inline arrays like `[1, 2]`), with no need for the **yaml** package.
R code tagged with `!expr` is evaluated unless you pass `envir = FALSE`:

```{r}
x = c("a: 1", "b: [1, 2]", "c: !expr 1 + 1", "d:", "  e: true")
str(taml_load(x))
str(taml_load(x, envir = FALSE))
```

## Read TAML from a file {#sec:taml-file}

`taml_file()` is `taml_load()` for a path:

```{r}
f = tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
writeLines(c("title: Hello", "tags: [\"a\", \"b\"]"), f)
str(taml_file(f))
```

## Write a list as TAML {#sec:taml-save}

`taml_save()` is the inverse. It returns the lines, or writes them to a file
when you give `path`:

```{r}
cfg = list(title = "Hi", n = 2, tags = c("a", "b"), sub = list(ok = TRUE))
taml_save(cfg)
f = tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
taml_save(cfg, f)
str(taml_file(f))
```

## Parse YAML with whatever is available {#sec:yaml-load}

`yaml_load()` uses the **yaml** package when it is installed and falls back to
`taml_load()` otherwise. Force the fallback with `use_yaml = FALSE`:

```{r}
yaml_load("a: 1\nb: [x, y]", use_yaml = FALSE)
```

## Split YAML metadata from the body {#sec:yaml-body}

`yaml_body()` splits a document into its front matter and the rest. The result
has the parsed `yaml`, its `lines` range, and the `body`, in which the YAML
lines are blanked so line numbers stay put. Use `parse = FALSE` to get the raw
YAML text:

```{r}
doc = c("---", "title: Hello", "---", "", "Content.")
str(yaml_body(doc))
yaml_body(doc, parse = FALSE)$yaml
```
